home.h1: The evidence on what causes cancer is public. Reading it shouldn't require a PhD.
home.lede: EpiDetective builds open instruments that turn epidemiological research into something you can interrogate yourself — for patients, clinicians, journalists, and the people who write policy.
purpose.label: What this is
purpose.p1: Each instrument here takes a body of evidence that already exists — usually rigorous, usually public, usually unreadable — and rebuilds it as something you can question directly. The work draws on cancer epidemiology, environmental and occupational health, causal inference, biostatistics and machine learning.
purpose.p2: The aim throughout is to translate without flattening: to make findings usable without quietly discarding the uncertainty that makes them honest.
inst.label: The instruments
inst.h2: One is open now. Others are being built.
inst.t1.name: Cancer Evidence Explorer
inst.t1.desc: Which exposures are linked to which cancers — and how certain each link actually is. Built directly on the World Health Organization's IARC Monographs, the most authoritative review of what can cause cancer. Start from a cancer, start from an exposure, or open the whole network.
inst.t2.name: Occupational Exposure Atlas
inst.t2.desc: What people are actually exposed to at work, and which of those exposures carry established cancer risk — drawing on job-exposure matrices from the SYNERGY and EPHOR cohorts.
inst.t3.name: Risk in Context
inst.t3.desc: A translator for the numbers that get misreported most: turning relative risks and hazard ratios into absolute terms a person can actually weigh.
about.label: Who builds this
about.h2: Built by a working cancer epidemiologist, not a content team.
about.p1: I am Wenxin Wan, a postdoctoral scientist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer — the World Health Organization's specialised cancer agency, in Lyon. My work sits where cancer epidemiology, causal inference, biostatistics and machine learning meet.
about.p2: I completed my PhD at Utrecht University's Institute for Risk Assessment Sciences, investigating occupational and environmental exposures and cancer risk. That work contributed evidence supporting the previously underrecognised causal role of benzene in lung cancer.
about.p3: I build these instruments because the evidence I work with every day is public and rigorous and almost unreadable unless you already know how to read it. That gap seemed worth closing.

foot.tagline: Translating science for a healthier world.
foot.disclaimer: EpiDetective publishes instruments for reading population-level evidence. Nothing here estimates individual risk, and nothing here is medical advice. Each instrument names its own sources.
exp.h1: Some exposures cause cancer. Some might. Telling them apart is the entire job.
exp.lede: Every mark behind this text is real: 185 exposures, 68 cancer types, and the 460 links the World Health Organization's cancer agency has documented between them.
exp.whatsin_h2: Every exposure the IARC has linked to a cancer site, graded by how sure we are.
exp.bar1_note: Human studies are consistent enough that chance, bias and confounding have been reasonably ruled out. This is the strongest statement the IARC makes.
exp.bar2_note: A credible association exists, but chance or bias cannot yet be excluded. Limited is not the same as harmless — it means the question is still open.
exp.reads_h2: Three things this map does not tell you.
exp.read1_h3: That something can cause cancer does not mean it caused yours.
exp.read1_p: A Group 1 classification means an exposure is capable of causing cancer under some conditions. How much, for how long, at what age, and with which genes all sit between that statement and any individual person.
exp.read2_h3: An absent link may mean nobody has looked hard enough yet.
exp.read2_p: The map records what has been studied and reviewed. Gaps are as often gaps in research funding and follow-up time as they are genuine absences of harm.
exp.read3_h3: This is a map of populations, not a verdict on a patient.
exp.read3_p: If you are living with a cancer diagnosis, the people treating you have information about your case that no population-level map contains. Bring questions to them.
exp.cta_h2: Start from a cancer. Start from an exposure. Or open the whole map.
exp.cta_lede: Free, no account, available in ten languages. Drag, zoom, and focus down to a single neighbourhood of the network.
exp.cta_source: Source: IARC Monographs, "Classifications by cancer site", Volumes 1–140, and Cogliano et al., JNCI 2011. This instrument presents population-level hazard identification. It does not estimate individual risk and is not medical advice.
